scope: Bounded primary-source corrections and profile requirements for the Asia/Pacific audit; not an exhaustive legal survey.

updates.reason: Do not equate the constitutional Hindi text with colloquial Fiji Hindi. Section 3 names Hindi; section 31(3) names conversational/contemporary Fiji Hindi for compulsory teaching. The latter is educational recognition, not proof that a separate hif official website profile is required.
Use the formal Hindi written profile for the constitutionally named Hindi standard. This is a written-profile mapping decision, not a denial of Fiji Hindi speakers or its educational recognition.
The constitution is published in English, iTaukei and Hindi; section 3 addresses the authoritative relationship of these texts.

English is now expressly statutory official under the English Language Act 2026. Earlier descriptions of it as only de facto official are outdated as of this audit date. Search-index text and parliamentary bill history confirm enactment; direct latest-text fetch returned 403.
Māori Language Act 2016 section 5 declares Māori official. This means New Zealand Māori, not Cook Islands Māori.
New Zealand Sign Language Act 2006 section 6 declares NZSL official. A written English or Māori JSON does not constitute an NZSL translation.
updates.translationGap: The current static text-only JSON model cannot faithfully deliver a signed language; video/sign-language presentation would be needed.

updates.reason: Papua New Guinea reported introduction of sign language as its fourth official language for government business in its 2016 national UPR report, launched 17 April 2015. Treat as the Papua New Guinean sign-language profile, not English text.
updates.translationGap: Requires sign-language media and an appropriate signed-language author.

updates.reason: Republic Act 11106 declares Filipino Sign Language the official sign language of government in transactions involving Deaf people. Its scope is explicit; it is not written Filipino.
updates.translationGap: Requires signed-language media; a Latin-script Filipino JSON is not FSL.

updates.reason: The 1987 Constitution Article XIV section 7 makes regional languages auxiliary official languages in their regions. This entry represents a regional-language candidate under that clause; the clause itself does not enumerate a closed language list.

Cook Islands national State of Environment report states that the Te Reo Maori Act 2003 recognizes Cook Islands Māori and English as official. New Zealand Māori mi is not a replacement. The statutory definition has broader dialect implications that need a separate full review.

The Niue Constitution has equally authoritative Niuean and English versions and Article 23 provides for Niuean and English in Assembly proceedings. This provides direct evidence of official written use.

Article 57 names French as the official language and gives Tahitian heritage/educational recognition. Do not label Tahitian co-official on that evidence; preserve it in a recognized-language note if desired.
Goa official-language law specifically requires Konkani in Devanagari; Marathi may also be used for official purposes. Romi Konkani is not an equivalent official script profile.

Uttarakhand official-language law provides Sanskrit as second official for notified purposes; Himachal Pradesh government documentation states second-official status from 21 May 2019. This is regional, not a Union official-language claim.

Government statements and Assam Assembly rules document Bodo as an associate official language following the 2020 amendment.
Basic Law Article 9 names Chinese and English, not a mandate for a separate colloquial written Cantonese profile. Traditional formal written Chinese with Hong Kong usage serves this written profile.

Macao government explicitly identifies Traditional Chinese and Portuguese versions as official-source content. A region tag must route to a Traditional Chinese profile under plain RFC4647 lookup; regional wording can reuse Hong Kong formal Chinese if reviewed.

Taiwan written Chinese uses Traditional characters. This profile covers its established administrative Chinese usage; it must not be described as excluding the national status accorded to other languages by the 2019 Act.

Mongolian Language Law sections 7.2 and 24.2 require state/local official affairs in Cyrillic and national script from 1 January 2025. Cyrillic mn alone does not cover explicit traditional-script requests.

notes.assessment: The Eighth Schedule lists 22 constitutionally scheduled languages; that status is not identical to Union or state official status. Do not mark all 22 as Union official. The regional additions above are examples backed by specific laws or government statements; this is not an exhaustive state-by-state legal enumeration.
notes.sourceGap: Current consolidated state/territory official-language laws and threshold notifications have not been exhaustively enumerated. Candidate tags are verification leads, not all asserted official.

notes.assessment: Chinese script/region profiles share the zh language identity. Mainland law names Putonghua and standardized characters; its revised law was adopted December 2025, so the older English translation is not the sole current reference. Hong Kong/Macao use the legal label Chinese; spoken Cantonese predominance does not alone mandate colloquial written Cantonese.
RFC4647 does not infer zh-TW or zh-HK to zh-Hant. Provide explicit region-tag files/aliases and script-region tags. CLDR likely-subtags can inform a catalog, but is not part of plain RFC4647 lookup.

The Development of National Languages Act gives equal national recognition to the natural languages of Taiwan ethnic groups and Taiwan Sign Language. This is broader than the administrative Chinese profile and should remain visible in recognized-language coverage; it is not a declaration that a Chinese JSON covers Taiwanese Hokkien, Hakka, indigenous languages or sign language.
notes.sourceGap: The scope includes national-language recognition and equal use rights, not merely administrative Mandarin. A complete list with current legal/community identity mappings remains to be established.

notes.assessment: Republic-era Article 16 sources are still hosted on official websites and name Dari/Pashto plus locally official languages, but the post-2021 de facto regime complicates their operative legal force. Label that basis historical/unresolved where appropriate. fa-af supplies a real Dari written profile; uz-arab would require Southern Uzbek rather than a Northern Uzbek respelling.
notes.sourceGap: Current operative legal status after 2021 is unresolved; Pashai, Nuristani and Pamiri legal labels additionally need individual-language mappings. Candidate tags are examples, not a closed interpretation of those group names.

notes.assessment: Punjab Assembly Rule 218 was expanded in 2024 to allow Punjabi, Saraiki, Potohari and Mewati alongside Urdu and English. Permission for assembly speeches is a narrower status than general provincial official-language designation. It does not establish a required pa-arab profile for this audit.
notes.sourceGap: Assembly-language permission does not settle general provincial official status.

notes.assessment: Hatohobei/Tobian and Sonsorolese state-official claims and Angaur Japanese should be checked against current state constitutions. A published scholarly article reproduces relevant clauses, but a current government-hosted primary text was not located in this bounded pass; keep these as unresolved verification leads, not silently covered by Palauan.
notes.sourceGap: Current government-backed texts of Sonsorol, Hatohobei and Angaur state constitutions remain to be verified.

notes.assessment: Cook Islands Māori, New Zealand Māori, Niuean, Tokelauan, Tuvaluan, Tahitian, Samoan and Tongan are not interchangeable files. Dictionary-supported spelling similarities do not establish translation equivalence.

notes.topic: Philippines auxiliary-regional umbrella not fully represented in CLDR
notes.assessment: The vendored CLDR PH data marks only ceb, hil, ilo, mdh, pag, tsg and war official_regional. It includes bik and pam without officialStatus and does not include bcl or mrw. Thus filtering CLDR on officialStatus does not exhaust the constitutional regional-language umbrella. This is a coverage-research gap; the Constitution does not itself supply a closed enumeration.
notes.sourceGap: Need a defensible mapping from languages actually regional in each part of the Philippines to Article XIV section 7, including individual versus macrolanguage distinctions. The candidate list is illustrative and not a declared legal roster.

notes.topic: Tagalog browser-tag compatibility with Filipino UI
notes.assessment: Full inspection of language/fil.json supports a declared tl-to-fil compatibility alias for these strings: ordinary Tagalog grammar and vocabulary with familiar technical loans. This is an implementation-specific equivalence of this UI text, not a declaration that the two language labels or all regional varieties are identical. Count it as reused translation content, not a new language translation.

Full review of the generic zh-hk error/challenge wording finds it suitable for a declared Macao compatibility alias. It is formal written Traditional Chinese, without colloquial Cantonese or Hong Kong-specific institutions. Describe it as reused formal Traditional Chinese, not an independently localized Macao translation.

speakerStatistics: No new speaker estimates asserted here. Keep L1, all-speaker, population-proxy, year and geographic-scope distinctions when the global audit merges its statistical sources.
